sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Vár** (*var*) — Agreement, Vow · Goddess of Oaths and Marriage Pacts — belongs to the Norse tradition, where she is catalogued under the domain "Oaths, Marriage Agreements". The name means "Agreement, vow".[^1]

Vár is one of the ásynjur, the female powers of the Norse pantheon, and is named in the Prose Edda as the goddess who hears the vows and agreements made between men and women, especially marriage contracts. Snorri explains her name as deriving from a word meaning 'vow' or 'pledge', and he adds that she punishes those who break their oaths. Her domain is therefore the sacred bond of speech — the promise that, once uttered, becomes a legal and moral reality.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Vár** and serves its temple at [vár.com](https://punicodex.com/var/). The restoration preserves the acute accent on the a that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *var* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Anthony Faulkes, Everyman / Viking Society for Northern Research, 1220.
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Vár.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Vár.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Old Norse as **Vár**. Etymologically it means "Agreement, vow"[^1]. The word *vár* is related to the concept of a pledge or contract, especially the marriage vow; it is also associated with spring (*vár*), and some scholars have debated whether the goddess's name is connected to the season of renewal. Snorri's etymology focuses on vows and agreements, making her the divine witness to human contracts.[^2]

The ASCII form *var* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Vár** recovers the acute accent of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries stress, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **v** → **V** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **á** — A with acute: stressed a
- **r** → **r** — Same

The project holds the domain **vár.com** as the canonical home of this name.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed., s.v. Vár.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/vaːr/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **V-** — Voiced labiodental fricative [v]
- **-á-** — Long open back [aː] with acute stress
- **-r** — Alveolar trill or tap [r]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'VAHR' — one syllable, with a long, stressed 'ah'.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Vár, the goddess of vows and marriage agreements
- **Modern Icelandic** — Vár, unchanged and still used as a given name

Vár is Tier 1 because the Norse form preserves the acute stress that ASCII loses. The restoration keeps that accent visible in the domain name.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Vár** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th–14th c. CE in the codices of Snorri's Edda, recording material centuries older.[^1] Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the Younger Futhark; no runic attestation of this name survives.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The normalized Old Norse spelling uses á (a with acute) for the long stressed vowel.
- In the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved approximately ᚢᛅᛦ, with the ᚢ-rune covering the v sound.
- The Unicode form **Vár** is a scholarly normalization that distinguishes the stressed long vowel from the plain ASCII form.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Vár** belongs to the Norse tradition as the goddess of vows, marriage agreements, and the spoken bond. Her domain is the moment when words become obligations and when two people or communities are joined by pledge.[^1]

### Marriage Vows

She hears the vows exchanged between bride and groom and holds the contract sacred.

### Oaths and Agreements

All formal pledges, especially those between men and women, fall under her gaze.

### Punishment of Perjury

Snorri says that she punishes those who break their vows, making her a judicial as well as a nuptial figure.

### Spring and Renewal

The homonymy of her name with the word for spring has led some scholars to associate her with seasonal renewal, though Snorri emphasizes the vow instead.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed., s.v. Vár.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Vár centers on the sacred bond and the spoken word:[^1]

- **The joined hands** — the handshake or clasp that seals a vow
- **The ring** — the circular pledge of marriage, without beginning or end
- **The drinking horn** — the shared cup of the wedding feast, drunk in honor of the gods
- **The contract or rune-stave** — the written or carved record of agreement
- **The spring flower** — a secondary emblem derived from the homonymy with 'spring'

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Vár's mythology is concentrated in a few sentences of Snorri's Prose Edda, but those sentences define a crucial domain: the sanctity of the spoken pledge.[^1]

### In the Prose Edda

In *Gylfaginning* 35 and in the þulur, Snorri lists Vár among the ásynjur and explains her name: 'She hears the vows and agreements that men and women make with each other; therefore the holy vows are called *várar*'. He adds that she punishes those who break their vows. The passage makes her the divine enforcer of contract, a function essential to a society in which legal agreements were often oral and witnessed by the community.[^2]

### Marriage and Law

In Old Norse society, marriage was a contractual arrangement between families, and the vows spoken at the wedding were binding on both parties and their kin. Vár's presence at such moments guaranteed that the pledge was heard by a power who could punish its breach. She thus bridges the domestic and the legal, the sacred and the social.[^3]

### Relation to Vǫr

Vár is often discussed alongside [[vor|Vǫr]], the goddess of hidden knowledge and oaths. The two names are sometimes confused in modern sources, but their functions differ: Vǫr knows secrets, while Vár witnesses vows, especially those of marriage. Together they form a pair of judicial goddesses guarding speech and truth.[^4]

Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, s.v. Vár.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Vár has no direct foreign counterpart, but the goddess who guards marriage vows has parallels in the Greek Hera Teleia, the Roman Juno, and the Germanic figure of Freyja as patroness of weddings. Within the Norse tradition she is closest to [[vor|Vǫr]], the goddess of oaths and hidden knowledge, and to [[frigg|Frigg]], the highest goddess associated with marriage and household.[^1]

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[vor|Vǫr]] and [[frigg|Frigg]], linked through oaths, marriage, and the sacred word.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Vár is remembered in modern Heathen and Ásatrú wedding rituals as the goddess who hears and guards vows. Her name is sometimes invoked when couples make their pledges, and she remains a figure for the idea that marriage is not merely a private feeling but a public and sacred contract.[^1] The name Vár is also a modern Icelandic given name, carrying the old sense of spring as well as the divine vow. In scholarship she is studied as one of the minor ásynjur whose functions illuminate the legal and religious status of marriage in Norse society.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, s.v. Vár.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: No cult site, votive deposit, or named image of Vár is known. Her attestation is entirely literary, confined to Snorri's Prose Edda. The relevant manuscripts are the principal codices of Snorri's Edda — the Codex Regius (GKS 2367 4to, early 14th c.), the Codex Wormianus, and the Uppsala Edda.[^1] The visual record is indirect: any image of a wedding scene or of a goddess receiving vows might evoke Vár, but no ancient image is labeled with her name.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (manuscript transmission).

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body: Vár is not named in the surviving Poetic Edda. Her attestation comes entirely from Snorri's prose, which may draw on lost eddic poems or on his own learned synthesis.[^1] The absence of a poetic narrative means that our picture of her is brief and schematic, concentrated in the etymology and attributes Snorri assigns to her.[^2]

sources.citation: Poetic Edda (Eddukvæði), ed. Neckel-Kuhn; trans. Carolyn Larrington, Oxford World's Classics (2014).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs.

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body: The Prose Edda is Vár's sole witness. In *Gylfaginning* 35 and in the þulur, Snorri lists her among the ásynjur and explains her name as 'vow' or 'agreement', adding that she hears the vows men and women make to each other and punishes those who break them.[^1] The passage is one of several in Snorri's catalog of goddesses that assigns a precise legal or social function to a minor deity, reflecting the learned, systematizing character of his handbook.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, s.v. Vár.

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body: The runic corpus contains no attestation of Vár. No runestone names her or uses her in a memorial formula.[^1] The name belongs to the mythographic vocabulary of the Prose Edda rather than to the commemorative world of the runic inscriptions. In the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved approximately ᚢᛅᛦ, but no such carving survives.[^2]

sources.citation: Rundata (Scandinavian Runic-text Database).
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body: Vár appears only rarely outside the Prose Edda. Later Icelandic learned tradition kept her name alive through copies of Snorri's Edda and through the prose summaries that accompanied skaldic verses. Saxo Grammaticus does not mention her, and she has no independent role in the family sagas.[^1] In modern retellings she is usually included as one of the minor ásynjur associated with marriage and oaths.[^2]

sources.citation: Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, Book 1, trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1979).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, s.v. Vár.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Vár is the witness to every promise. She does not speak the vow; she hears it, and in her hearing it becomes real. In an age when contracts are often reduced to fine print and promises to performance metrics, she reminds us that the spoken word was once sacred enough to require a goddess. The restoration of her name in Unicode is a small act of recognition for the old conviction that a vow, once made, binds both speaker and world.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
